baseline.statement: You told us your client base is steady. What keeps it steady is usually a handful of relationships and habits only you can name.

baseline.statement: How you decide what to charge is almost certainly yours alone — it usually is, and nothing you told us suggests otherwise.

baseline.statement: You told us roughly $4,200,000 through the door and about $620,000 of that as owner earnings. The statements behind those sit with your accountant; what a buyer needs is the story linking them.

baseline.statement: Your revenue leans on a handful of key clients and some of it is contracted or repeat. Who holds those relationships is the part a buyer asks about first.

sections.title: What the business owns
sections.question: Owned vs leased vs personally held; deferred maintenance; whether the premises lease transfers.
sections.ownerQuestion: What do you own, what do you lease, and what is held in your own name?

baseline.statement: You told us about $480,000 of equipment, vehicles and stock. The register and the finance paperwork are usually at the accountant's or in a drawer.

sections.title: Licences, insurance and the calendar
sections.question: The obligations calendar and who watches it; change-of-control clauses; anything in dispute.
sections.ownerQuestion: What must not lapse, and who is watching it?

sections.title: Systems & records
sections.question: Where records live, who has access, what is documented, and whether the IP is owned by the entity.
sections.ownerQuestion: Where do your records live, who can reach them, and what is written down?

baseline.statement: Which tools the business actually depends on — and who holds the logins — is not something you have told us yet.

everythingHeld.content: Gary is the leading hand with 24 years experience and is the only other person who can price a job; he is 61. Sharon handles invoicing, payroll and ATO work three days a week and is Ray's sister-in-law. Dylan is a fourth year apprentice and Ray wants to keep him. Only Gary knows the mine site loading. Nobody knows Ray is thinking of selling.
Systematising and documenting essential work steps will help the business function during staff absences and improve saleability.
Mapping critical roles and processes currently performed only by the owner or Gary and delegating them to other staff will support business continuity.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Delegating critical owner roles for continuity

everythingHeld.content: Systematising and documenting essential work steps is needed to allow the business to function if key people are unavailable.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Document essential work steps for continuity

everythingHeld.content: Capturing and formalising Gary's specific pricing knowledge, especially about mine site loading, is necessary to reduce knowledge risk.
A map of critical roles and processes that only the owner or Gary perform should be created, with a plan to train or delegate these tasks to others to ensure business continuity.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Critical roles held by owner and Gary

everythingHeld.content: A documented pricing process including margin structures and exceptions is essential to improve business transparency and buyer confidence.
A plan to capture and formalize key pricing knowledge Gary holds, especially relating to mine site loading, should be created to reduce knowledge concentration risk.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Plan to formalize key pricing knowledge

everythingHeld.content: Only a few staff members, including Gary, Sharon, and Dylan, hold critical operational knowledge, indicating limited knowledge distribution.
A pricing summary document has been drafted and is ready to be sent or saved upon approval from the owner.
Pricing models for service and tendered work are mentally held and not documented, complicating buyer trust and business replication.
Staff with critical operational knowledge are few, creating risks around reliance on key individuals.
The business knowledge and pricing authority are concentrated mainly in two people, the owner and Gary, which risks operational dependency.
Critical knowledge, especially pricing knowledge held by Gary, is not captured or formalized in writing.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Pricing knowledge held only by Gary

everythingHeld.content: Pricing models for both service and tendered work are not documented and exist only mentally, reducing trust and replicability for buyers.
The business heavily depends on only two people, the owner and Gary, for pricing jobs and critical operational knowledge such as mine site loading.

Staff details: Gary is leading hand, 24 years with the business, only other person who can price jobs, age 61. Sharon handles invoicing, payroll, and ATO work part-time (3 days/week), sister-in-law. Dylan is a fourth-year apprentice and preferred to keep. Only Gary knows mine site loading details. Nobody knows about the owner's intention to sell.

Pricing model: Service work charged at $118/hr plus materials at cost plus 22%. Tendered jobs have labour and materials plus 18% margin, except mine sites have 28% margin due to standdowns and inductions. Builders with long-term relationships on straightforward jobs get a 12% margin. Mental calculation based on drawings, not documented.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Service and tender job pricing margins

everythingHeld.content: Pricing approach: Service work is charged at $118 per hour plus materials at cost plus 22%. Tendered jobs: Labour and materials computed then add 18% margin, except for mine sites where margin is 28% due to standdowns and inductions. For builders with long-term relationships and straightforward jobs, margin is reduced to 12%. This pricing is not documented and is mentally calculated based on drawings.
everythingHeld.genome_headline: Service and tender pricing margins detailed

everythingHeld.content: What he said he wants to work on, in his own words when he set me up: I run a commercial electrical and mechanical contracting business I started 35 years ago. I am starting to think about selling in the next two to five years and almost nobody knows. I want to get what is in my head written down so the business is worth something without me.

Your own valuation, from the thirteen questions you answered before signing up (Electrical & Mechanical Contracting): worth today $1,700,000, worth once your knowledge is captured $1,970,000, so the gap is $271,000.
